cases.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1 and 2/16 expressed in fractional notation converts to 1.125
cases.expected_note: Excel documents this example's result as 1.125. The fractional part .02 is read as 2 sixteenths: 1 + 2/16 = 1.125

cases.description: Documented example: 1.1 in thirty-seconds notation is 1 and 10/32
cases.expected_note: Excel documents this example's result as 1.3125. The fractional digits are padded to the width of the fraction denominator: .1 means 10 thirty-seconds, so 1 + 10/32 = 1.3125

cases.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a non-integer fraction is documented as truncated to an integer
cases.expected_note: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is not an integer, it is truncated.' Truncating 16.9 to 16 reproduces the first documented example exactly, 1.125. An engine that rounded 16.9 to 17, or used it as-is, would return a different value

cases.description: A negative fractional dollar keeps its sign through the conversion
cases.expected_note: The magnitude converts the same way as the documented positive example and the sign is preserved: -(1 + 2/16) = -1.125

cases.description: A fraction denominator of zero cannot be divided by
cases.expected_note: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is greater than or equal to 0 and less than 1, DOLLARDE returns the #DIV/0! error value.' Note the band is 0 <= fraction < 1, which is worded more widely than DOLLARFR's page (which names only fraction = 0) even though truncation makes the two equivalent in practice

cases.description: A negative fraction denominator is outside the documented domain
cases.expected_note: Excel documents #NUM! if fraction is less than 0
